Alice — thanks for the clear list. Pasting a concise proposal below so your legal/procurement teams have something to react to right away. We'll schedule time if you want to walk through specifics.

PROPOSAL HIGHLIGHTS (summary for addendum)
- Reserved capacity: N-8 GPUs (A100-class equivalent), with baseline throughput guarantee of 12k tokens/sec across the pool for steady-state inference (measured at service edge).
- Headroom: additional burst capacity up to +30% of baseline for sustained windows of up to 15 minutes; automated scaling beyond that subject to capacity availability.
- Latency SLOs: 95th percentile < 120ms, 99th percentile < 320ms for interactive requests (seq length <= 256) under steady-state.
- Latency fallback: if 99th percentile breaches thresholds for > 10 continuous minutes we will automatically route new requests to an agreed compatible model (e.g., quantized variant) and issue token credits equal to estimated affected tokens (credit calculation: tokens_sent * 1.2).
- Queueing safeguards: interactive requests tagged with priority header (x-rdw-priority: interactive) receive preemptive scheduling within the Dedicated pool; nightly batch jobs are run in reserved low-priority slices and are subject to preemption to protect interactive traffic.
- Observability & tracing: we will provide per-route latency histograms, token-level billing, and a sampling of trace ids for incidents.
- Maintenance & failover: scheduled maintenance windows will be communicated 72 hours in advance; cross-region failover can be invoked with a 30-minute RTO for stateless workloads.

Next steps: attached is a first-pass term sheet (proposed-warranty-term-v1.pdf). Ben / Mark, could you confirm the baseline numbers and the credit math? Naomi, can you prepare the billing/credits language for the addendum? Alice, if these look directionally correct, happy to set a call Wed morning.

Technical clarifications for queueing and fallback behavior:

- Preemption model: Dedicated pool uses a two-tier scheduler. Interactive work is kept in a low-latency lane. Batch jobs are scheduled in background slices; when preemption occurs we checkpoint batch progress and resume in the next low-util window.
- KV cache implications: switching to a quantized fallback model will clear model-specific KV caches; warmup will impact tail latency for the first ~500 tokens. To mitigate, we suggest a small warmup buffer (warmup requests primed 5 minutes pre-failover) and a short TTL on cold cache buckets.
- Observability hooks: we can provide real-time alerts (via webhook) for rolling 10-minute 99th percentile breaches and per-request trace ids. Please see our internal ticket for the runbook: JIRA SUP-4217.

If Zenox needs deterministic cold-start guarantees, that requires pinned warmup instances (additional charge). Otherwise the fallback approach above is the pragmatic compromise to keep costs predictable.
